image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Horizontal bar chart / progress-bar style chart**
- Each row shows the **share who are women** as a filled horizontal bar, with a numeric label inside the bar and a separate right-aligned number for **total workers**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel ranked list** of categories.
- **No faceting** or small multiples.
- Uses **aligned horizontal bars** by category.
- The bars are effectively **part-to-whole/progress bars**: purple filled portion for the women’s share against a light gray full-length background.
- A horizontal divider separates **“All essential workers”** from the occupation-specific rows.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / worker group (e.g., Social workers, Health care, Critical retail, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; left-side text labels |
| Share who are women (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal bar length (purple fill); numeric text label inside bar |
| Total workers | Quantitative | Right-side numeric text label |
| All essential workers vs. specific occupations | Categorical/nominal | Separate row placement; horizontal divider indicating grouping |

comments.raw_comment: After analyzing the graph, I notice that the majority of essential workers are women, with a 52% share. Essential occupations such as resource extraction, farmers, and law enforcement have a majority of men, which may stem from previous social beliefs about occupations for women. One statistic that surprises me is the health care and social care share, which display a majority of women in that field. Even through acts of oppression throughout the 20th century, women are able to receive the majority of essential jobs in our nation, but this doesn’t coordinate with another statistic. Although women take the majority of essential occupations, does their compensation coordinate with their importance in these occupations? Due to previous acts of oppression, it has been an ongoing issue that is still debated. Regardless of the reasoning, women have and will remain an important aspect of the American workforce.

I also wonder why there are only 11% of women in resource extraction. This does not have much of an impact on me- at least not yet. This does have a pretty big impact on females that work, the ratio of males to females can affect how they work, how much they're paid, and how they're treated. A catchy headline could be, "The Female Force".

comments.raw_comment: I think this graph is very interesting, and frankly, almost exactly what I would have predicted it to look like. The gender stereotypes I have grown up with and been exposed to are apparent even in the occupational differences between women and men. The medical field and social sciences have always seemed more feminine to me, rather than law enforcement and defense, which appear more predominantly male. I believe a good question to ask ourselves, though, is if this separation of genders in the workplace is inherently bad. Personally, I would argue that no, these differences are not harmful to either gender. They can become detrimental, though, when certain stigmas or stereotypes are enforced because of mere statistics. For example, to say that women only belong in the health fields because they are not capable of anything else, is not only wrong, but also extremely limiting to young girls as they consider their futures. I think that each person should be challenging themselves to think outside of the societal norms that have been in place for decades, encouraging the breakdown of these barriers. No woman, or man, should feel inferior or superior to another simply because of their occupation. I believe it is time to begin challenging the status quo of women in the workforce, encouraging this nation’s young girls to explore their true desires, not those that have been predetermined for them.

comments.raw_comment: I notice that out of all essential workers right now, women only make up the majority as healthcare and social workers. The total amount of healthcare workers is much larger than any other essential career field currently, so it is important that women make up such a larger percentage of that group. However besides those two fields and also critical research, women are a minority in every other field of essential workers. I wonder what causes such a drastic difference in gender inequality within the different fields. How are women taking up such a large majority in certain fields, but hardly work in any other fields at all? This graph impacts me because as a woman, it concerns me that in the majority of these fields, women's presence is very limited and it is upsetting to see there is still such strong gender inequality and stigmas in society. Although on the other hand, it is inspiring to see women taking charge in a few of these career fields, because I feel as though a graph comparing these fields from 2000 or 2010 would likely show even lower percentages in women in any of these fields. comments.raw_comment: I noticed that just over half of all essential workers are women. However, only 3 of the jobs listed have over 50% of its workers as women. As you follow the list of jobs down, the percentage of women in that job decreases. I noticed that this pattern follows a pattern of stereotypical jobs. Jobs such as law enforcement, transit/transportation, defense, can be considered as "manly" jobs.  The jobs that have the largest percentages of female workers cater towards health and social services. I feel that these fields are more associated towards the nurturing character of women. I wonder if less women are in law enforcement, defense, etc. because less women apply to such jobs or if more women are rejected from those jobs. In addition, I wonder why most women work as in health care, critical retail, and social work. I also wonder what this graph would like if these bars were then separated by ethnicity. It would also be interesting to tie this graph to the level of education that workers receive. Lastly, I wonder how accurate this graph is, seeing as it's taken from 2014-2018. This impacts my community because it shows how women are equally as essential to the workforce as men, and in some cases, dominate specific fields. You can also relate this to today and to the most common majors that students choose for their studies. It also shows all the different jobs that are considered essential to our community. I would headline this as "An Essential Reminder About Essential Women."

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that women make up a little more than half of the essential worker population. I also noticed that most of the women are social and health care workers. In total, there are 21,410,000 people who hold those jobs and only 16,508,900 are women. It also looks like the percentage of working women decreases from handling medical supplies to resource extraction. I wonder about which states or cities this data came from as well as the pay difference between the men and women who work these jobs. I wonder about how the percentages changed from before the pandemic and how it will be affected once it is over.  Lastly, it’ll be intriguing to learn about the difference in pay for women who are social workers and those who do resource extraction. The impact this topic has on me is quite huge. I am a female, currently in my junior year of high school deciding what career I want to do in the future. This graph opened my eyes to the many essential jobs in the country and gives me an idea of the different careers I can put myself into. The impact this topic has on my community is that there are women within my community who are essential workers. There are also young female adults who are currently looking for jobs or are on their way to pursuing their careers having one of them categorized as essential work. If they choose essential work that is not usually picked up by women, it could change the outlook of jobs that are usually picked up by men.

comments.raw_comment:
1. I notice that the graph starts with a general percentage of the total amount of female essential workers in the U.S. The bar chart lists the essential jobs with higher percentages of females towards the top, and the jobs with less females towards the bottom. I notice that essential social workers have the largest percentage while resource extraction is the smallest percentage. The health care bar is something else I notice because it has the second highest percentage of females in the study and it has the largest amount of total workers out of all the data. 

2. I wonder what makes a job more appealing to a female than a man? For professions such as social work or health care, there is an overwhelming amount of females than males. Why are those jobs more desirable to women? Why is Defense or Resource Extraction less popular to women? Is it a similar factor in each of these jobs that makes it more appealing to a women? 

3. The impact this has on my community and I is it could encourage the next generation to prove this data wrong. A young boy could become a social worker or a nurse and lower the percentage of females in the job after seeing how few men are involved. A little girl could be motivated to raise the percentage of females in jobs at the bottom of the graph. It pushes us to prove the stereotypes wrong, and promote the idea that gender does not qualify someone for a job. 

 4. A catchy headline could be, "Essential Workers? How about Essential Females"

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that a large amount of social, health care, and critical retail workers are female. However, after that, the percentage tends to drop. In the careers that tend to require less education, there seems to be fewer women, but this is not always the case.
I wonder why women are attracted to jobs in social work in health care. Is it because women tend to prefer jobs where they are able to help or nurture others? I also wonder why fewer women take up jobs that require less education. Is it because in certain areas, women are not expected to have to work and they could simply stay at home should they not have received a higher education?
This has a large impact not only on my community, but also on my life as a girl. Although the only jobs represented are essential work, the gender gap is prevalent in many different job fields (and not only for women!). If I wanted to be a university professor at a top institution, I would likely be outnumbered by men. The percentage of female artists in the met modern art section is less than 20%. Fewer than 20% of engineers are female. But in my community, this shows the small number of people who had to work and put their health at risk. I commend them for their selflessness and overall chivalry.
My title would be, "Our Essential Workers; Our Essential Women".

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that there is a higher percentage of women working in white-collar jobs than in blue-collar jobs. Assuming that Social workers, Health care, Medical supplies, and Financial IT are all white-collar jobs and the rest are blue-collar and that the numbers in the middle were the percent of women in the job, then 75.59% of the 22,290,000 white-collar workers, are women. However, women only hold 31.09% of 26,500,000 blue-collar jobs. 

I also noticed that when you add up all of the total workers on the right side of the graph, they equal 48,790,000, as opposed to the 48,710,000 that are all the essential workers. I thought that maybe the percent of total essential workers that are women would be different, but after finding the amount of women for all of the individual types of jobs and then adding them up and dividing them by the total number of workers, I got 52% which was what the graph had originally said. 

I wonder where the extra 80,000 workers came from when adding the number of workers on the right. 
I wonder why there are more women in white-collar jobs than in blue-collar.
Lastly, I wonder how accurate these numbers are today, and how much they have changed from this 2014-2018 survey.

I think this graph could be called: "Are Essential jobs need Essential Woman."

comments.raw_comment: I notice that the number of women that are essential workers is slightly above half, but that only 3 of the jobs were greater than 50% (social workers health care workers, and critical retail workers). When the other 11 jobs were less than 50%, with 5 of them being less than 20% percent. I also notice that there is a prevalent difference in the percentage of female workers within stereotypical areas, for example, social work is often considered more "feminine",  and is nearly 80% women. On the other side of the spectrum financial IT services (28%), and defense (14%) 2 more stereotypically "masculine" professions. I wonder how the amount of women in these professions (and others) have changed especially in the last 50 or so years, and this year when considering the global pandemic. I wonder if this study is only those who were assigned female at birth (which would include those who are trans female to male and female to nonbinary or any other identity of those who are assigned female at birth) or those who identify as female (which would include transwomen and not include transmen and people under the umbrella term of nonbinary). On the same note I wonder whether the women in these positions were influenced to fill them because of stereotypes. A good title for this graph would be "More Women Than Anyone Else Are Working as Essential Workers".

comments.raw_comment: I notice that although the graph of all essential workers shows that 52% of workers are women, the distribution of women within the different sectors of work is widely varied. This being said, I wonder if woman essential workers are unproportionally contracting COVID at their workplace compared to their male counterparts. It also makes me wonder if we're going to see a shrink in the social work and healthcare work force, as I've seen headlines saying that women are quitting their jobs to take care of young children. I would say this graph tells me that in my Maryland suburb with a lot of nearby hospitals and health centers, there are probably a lot of kids who's mothers are working on-site rather than from home. If their husbands (in heterosexual relationships) are also working on-site or busy on their work-from-home workload, there is a huge need for comprehensive child care. A catchy headline would be: "Case managers, IT workers, and welders: how gendered expectations of occupation may affect COVID contraction risk among men and women".

comments.raw_comment: I notice that while 52% of essential workers are women, men dominate more than 75% of the fields. Women completely dominate 78% of social work and 77% health care. However, the number of women drop in the other fields where they are greatly dominated by men, such as defense, law enforcement, farmers, and IT services. I wonder if this is due to hiring practices or a belief held by women that they can't pursue careers in these fields. This also can be a sign that men aren't as encouraged to pursue careers in the non-doctoral (?) medicine and caring fields as women are. I also wonder if the graph is misleading. The graph shows how many of the workers in that field are women but doesn't really include data about the total number. With differing sizes in workforces for different fields, the data may be interpreted differently with more information added. I also am not sure if the "Total Workers" column to the right refers to the number of women or actual total including men, which could help answer my previous question. This impacts me and my community because it can inform us of the disparities between different genders in different fields. School and human resource programs can use this information to level the playing field and encourage more men and women to join fields not dominated by their genders. A possible catchy headline is "Women Dominate Essential Workers...or do they?" or "Essential Workers: Are both genders essential?"

1. I notice that of all the essential workers, about half of them are women. There is a 2 percent difference between women and men, but it's fairly even between them. However, in most of the subgroups of essential workers, men have the majority. In fact, in all categories (bar social workers, health care workers, and critical retailers), the majority of the workers are men.

2. This leads me to wonder two things: number one, WHY do there seem to be more non-women in the essential work field, and since there is, HOW is it that women still have a slight majority in the collective number of essential workers?

When I look closer, I can see the total number of workers in each field (on the right side of the graph). This explains my second question, but I still want to know why so many women are skewed towards being a social worker or helath care professional, and so few towards resource extraction, law enforcement, farming, and other occupations near the bottom of the graph.

Or maybe that's just my introversion talking.

3. This has a huge impact on our community. It shows the ratio of women to men in a variety of essential careers. It could also give college students an idea as to what they may or may not wish to major in.

4. A catchy headling for this graph could be: "Women are Essential! (and Men Are Too): The Skew Between Genders In Essential Careers".

I noticed that although out of the total number of essential workers women only take up 4% more than men, the data is extremely varied across all occupations, ranging from 11% in resource extraction to 78% of social workers. Personally, I was shocked when I also noticed that women constitute 77% of the healthcare workforce, which is nearly 40% of all essential occupations.
	I wonder why teaching and education have not been included in the essential works list, and if they were, what would the share of women in that area be? Would that data entry drive the average percentage of women in the essential workforce upwards? If yes, that (alongside their share in healthcare) would once again show us just how incredibly important women’s jobs really are and the degree to which our entire society relies on them.
	At the moment, this particular topic has a tremendous impact on the entire nation, including me and the community in which we live. In a time when the majority of the workforce is slowly just starting to come back to work, it is the essential workers who have been carrying all of us on their backs by working on the frontlines in spite of all the risks — the vast majority of them were women. Now, it is our responsibility to remember their effort and be thankful for their unconditional desire to help everyone else.
	Finally, a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea would be “Who are our frontline workers?”
